3: Step one: load the data and scale it. We read the wine C S V, take the first eleven columns as the lab measurements, and scale them with standard scaler so every column has mean zero and standard deviation one. P C A follows the largest variance. Total sulfur dioxide has a standard deviation of fifty six point five two before scaling, free sulfur dioxide seventeen point seven five, alcohol one point one nine, and density point zero zero three. After scaling all are one. Without scaling, PC one would explain ninety five percent only because sulfur dioxide has the biggest numbers.
4: Step two: check multicollinearity with V I F. The V I F is the diagonal of the inverse correlation matrix, the same result as running eleven separate regressions. Density has a V I F of fifteen point nine one, over ten, so serious. Residual sugar seven point two three, fixed acidity four point nine, alcohol four point seven eight, total sulfur dioxide two point nine four, down to sulphates one point five four. Drop density and the largest V I F is two point eight four. P C A components always have V I F equal to one.
5: Step three: fit P C A. P C A with no arguments keeps all eleven components, and fit transform learns the axes and gives each wine its principal component values. We put them in a data frame called P C one to P C eleven. The correlation between components is the identity matrix, ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere. The data is still six thousand four hundred ninety seven by eleven. P C A only rotates the axes, and the new columns are uncorrelated, so there is no repeated information.
6: Step four: variance explained. We build a table of the eigenvalue, the percentage explained, and the cumulative percentage. An eigenvalue is the variance carried by a principal component. With scaled data the total is eleven, one per feature. PC one: eigenvalue three point oh three, twenty seven point five percent. PC two: two point four nine, twenty two point seven, cumulative fifty point two. PC three: one point five six, fourteen point one, sixty four point four. PC four: eight point eight percent, seventy three. PC five: seventy nine point seven. PC six: eighty five point three. PC seven: ninety point zero. So PC one plus PC two is fifty percent, and seven components reach ninety percent.
7: The scree plot and cumulative plot. A bar chart of the percentage explained shows an elbow after PC three. A line of the cumulative percentage crosses the ninety percent line, drawn in red, at seven components.
8: How many components to keep? Count eigenvalues greater than one, which gives three. And fit P C A with n components equal to point nine, which means keep enough components for ninety percent of the variance, which gives seven. The rules: the elbow keeps three, for a quick look. Kaiser, eigenvalue above one, keeps three, for scaled data. A variance target of ninety percent keeps seven, to keep most of the information.
9: Step six: loadings, what each component is made of. We take the first three rows of the components matrix, transposed, and draw a heat map. PC one: white style, with sulfur dioxide and sugar, versus red style, with volatile acidity and chlorides. PC two: heavy, density, versus light, alcohol. PC three: acidity, citric and fixed, versus pH.
10: Step seven: plot each wine on PC one and PC two, coloured by type. The average position for red wines is PC one minus two point five one and PC two point seven eight. For white wines, PC one point eight two and PC two minus point two five. P C A never saw the type, yet red and white separate along PC one, so the name red versus white style is right.
11: Step eight: the loading plot, showing how the features point. Arrows start at the origin, zero zero, and end at each feature's loading on PC one and PC two, drawn in one quiver command, no loop. Same direction means rise together, like the two sulfur dioxides. Opposite means one up, one down, like density versus alcohol.
